In the 2nd and 3rd centuries, the old Roman religion faced pressure from many new religious movements - Christianity was just the one that prevailed. You also had the cult of Sol Invictus - the Unconquered Sun - which was very popular around that time. In fact, Constantine the Great, who is popularly remembered for being the first Christian emperor, actually seemed to be hedging his bets by paying respect to Sol Invictus as well, portraying the deity on his official coinage, building monuments, and naming 'Sunday' - the day of the Sun - an official day of rest in the empire. Incidentally, the festival of the birth of the Unconquered Sun was December 25. The cult of Mithras is another example, which was picked up around this time from the Persians.

The Romans were never really about converting conquered people to the pagan Roman religion - they would sometimes draw associations between native gods and their own (e.g. Jupiter/Zeus), but they would by-and-large allow conquered peoples to practice their own religion. Their only religious demand of their subjects was that they worship the emperor himself as a living deity (which Jews and Christians refused to do, hence the root of their historically acrimonious relations with the Romans). The Roman religion wasn't really international in scope - it was really all about the sacred city of Rome itself, and the sacred practices necessary to ensure its survival and prosperity. Non-Romans were not really included.

This meant that later on, as the empire as an institution gained a unified identity that wasn't really "Roman", per se, there was a religious vacuum to be filled. If it wasn't Christianity, it would have been something else, probably similar in many ways.
